name: Na
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Only van Driem 2001:489 and Blench & Post 2011 mention Na (nbt) in passing per Glottolog; no grammar or phonology located

sources.citation: Post, Mark W. 2011. Prosody and typological drift in Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman: Against 'Indosphere' and 'Sinosphere'. In Srichampa, Sidwell & Gregerson (eds.), Austroasiatic Studies: papers from ICAAL 4 (Mon-Khmer Studies Special Issue 3), 198-221.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Family-level only, Na not named: 'although all known Tani languages appear to exhibit a falling rhythm and agglutinating morphological profile, there is an uneven distribution of trochaic effects.. The greatest evidence for trochaic effects is found in Upper Belt Nyishi, a Western Tani language' (p.214-215); 'we continue to lack adequate data for the majority of Tani languages'. Not a statement about Na.

sources.citation: Sun, Jackson T.-S. 1994. Linguistic Characteristics of the Tani (Mirish) Branch of Tibeto-Burman. Bulletin of the Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica 65(1).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); the open copy could not be downloaded when a reader tried
sources.note: Sun's typological survey of Tani built on his own Na Bengni (= Na of Taksing) and Bokar field data; likeliest open source to contain a general prosody/stress remark for Na Bengni. Free PDF on the IHP site but the file host (www11.ihp.sinica.edu.tw) times out by automated download and the only Internet Archive copy is truncated/unreadable.

sources.citation: Post, Mark W. 2015. Tones in Northeast Indian languages, with a focus on Tani: A fieldworker's guide. In Post, Morey & DeLancey (eds.), Language and Culture in Northeast India and Beyond (Asia-Pacific Linguistics 023), 182-211. Canberra.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Na stress. Table 5 lists 'Bangni (in Tibet)' under 'Conflicting reports' for tone; fn.5: Ou-Yang (1985) claimed no tone in Bengni, 'T. Sun (1993) later found that this was not the case of Bengni, at least, in which at least some clear minimal pairs on tone were found.' General Tani syllable-weight discussion only.

sources.citation: Sun, T.-S. Jackson. 2003. Tani languages. In G. Thurgood & R. LaPolla (eds.), The Sino-Tibetan Languages (1st ed.), 456-466. London: Routledge (archive.org djvu text excerpt).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. States '(Na) Bengni and Bokar data in this chapter are from my personal research conducted in Tibet'; phonology section covers vowels/length ('In Bokar and Bengni, vowels contrast in length regardless of position in a word'), codas, and tone: 'In one type of Na Bengni, for example, high-low pitches need to be lexically marked for certain words.. In another Bengni dialect, interestingly, the same words are distinguished by vowel qualities'.

sources.citation: Sun, Jackson T.-S. 1993. The linguistic position of Tani (Mirish) in Tibeto-Burman: a lexical assessment. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 16(2): 143-188. doi:10.15144/LTBA-16.2.143 (sealang.net archive).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing; lexical subgrouping paper condensed from ch. V of the dissertation (scanned PDF, no text layer; pp.1-8 scanned to confirm scope). Uses Bengni S (Na Bengni) forms but has no phonological description.

sources.citation: Sun, Tianshin Jackson. 1993. A Historical-Comparative Study of the Tani (Mirish) Branch in Tibeto-Burman. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley (2007 re-typeset PDF, 471 pp., formerly hosted at ling.sinica.edu.tw; downloaded via the Internet Archive 20160304103740).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in (also digitized at HathiTrust, search-only (in copyright))
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 1.5.2 'Phonemic Inventories of the Key Languages', (2) Bengni S [= Na Bengni, the speech of the Na tribe of the Taksing area, per appendix pp.423-424], PDF pp.30-32 gives onsets, clusters, vowels ('Vowel length is contrastive in open syllables'), codas, a remark that high vowels 'are devoiced when they are preceded by voiceless onsets in the second syllable of a disyllabic word; the vowel in the first syllable may be optionally lengthened', and '5. Tonality: Na Bengni seems to have developed a marginal tone system which has not yet become fully functional in the entire lexicon.…

sources.citation: Post, Mark W. & Jackson T.-S. Sun. 2017. Tani languages. In Graham Thurgood & Randy J. LaPolla (eds.), The Sino-Tibetan Languages, 2nd edition, 322-337. London: Routledge.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, paywalled at the publisher (DOI); library e-access not checked
sources.note: Most recent authoritative family overview by the two specialists; names 'Na/Bangni' in its prosody discussion (tone) and, given Post's work on Tani trochaic word rhythm, probably states word-level stress/rhythm for Western Tani including Na/Bangni.

sources.citation: Pertin, Kabuk. 1994. Nah Language Guide. Itanagar: Directorate of Research, Government of Arunachal Pradesh. 106 pp.

sources.note: The only published description devoted to Na/Nah itself (Glottolog's sole descriptive reference); language guides of this series open with a sound-system section that occasionally comments on tone/stress.

sources.citation: Ouyang Jueya 欧阳觉亚. 1985. 珞巴族语言简志(崩尼-博嘎尔语) [Brief description of the Luoba language: Bengni-Bokar]. Beijing: Minzu chubanshe.

sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Chinese jianzhi whose Bengni phonemic inventory was recorded from a Na speaker from Taksing (Sun 1993:422-424); jianzhi phonology chapters routinely include a sentence on 重音 (stress), and pp.11-12 discuss weakly articulated prefixal syllables.

sources.citation: Post, Mark W. 2013. Defoliating the Tani Stammbaum: An exercise in areal linguistics. Paper presented at the 13th Himalayan Languages Symposium, ANU Canberra, 9 Aug 2013 (academia.edu 4167715).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Post's comparative paper that treats Na as a Bangni lect; may contain Na field data with prosodic transcription, though a stress statement is unlikely.

sources.citation: Ouyang Jueya 欧阳觉亚. 1985. 珞巴族语言简志(崩尼-博嘎尔语) Luobazu yuyan jianzhi (Bengni-Boga'er yu) [Brief description of the Luoba nationality language: Bengni-Bokar]. Beijing: Minzu chubanshe. (HathiTrust uc1.31822026337816, search-only.)
sources.tag: not read: abstract or record only
sources.note: Not seen. Per Sun 1993:422-424 its Bengni phonemic inventory was 'recorded at Rtsedthang with a male speaker of Bengni from Taksing', i.e. Na (naaa1245); Sun 1993:52 cites Ouyang 1985:11-12 on weakly pronounced prefix syllables whose vowel quality depends on speech tempo (a prosodic remark, language unspecified, probably Bokar).
